full_text:
Jason Arday, the Cambridge professor accused of plagiarism and embellishment, is to face investigation by the university after it said it received “new information” about his qualifications and career.

Cambridge initially defended Arday – the youngest black professor appointed in the university’s history, with a compelling life story of educational disadvantage – as “the victim of a vile campaign”. But as questions mounted over Arday’s own claims, the university’s leaders felt that Cambridge’s reputation was in danger.

The Guardian published its own investigation uncovering discrepancies in Arday’s public accounts involving prodigious fundraising feats as well as claims he had been targeted by knife-wielding masked intruders.

Arday first faced allegations that he plagiarised parts of his PhD thesis and other academic research late last year, and has rejected the claims. An investigation by Liverpool John Moores University, which awarded his PhD in 2015, did not uphold the charges of plagiarism but said they were probably caused by “honest and reasonable error”.

Arday has denied plagarism, telling the Guardian last week: “There have been multiple thorough investigations across several institutions as a result of the allegations, and immense scrutiny, including with an academic misconduct panel who concluded that there was no plagiarism or academic misconduct.”

The statement from the university on Wednesday evening said: “The University of Cambridge has begun an investigation following new information about Prof Arday’s academic qualifications and honorary appointments. In order to ensure a fair process, we will not comment further until this has concluded.

“Separately, there remains a number of ongoing complaints regarding academic misconduct, which are being handled in line with our misconduct in research policy. This is consistent with our previous statement on the matter.

“While we are fully aware of the public commentary and concerns around this matter, it remains vital that any process is thorough and adheres to both university policies and employment law.

“We also fully recognise that there is a person at the centre of this situation, and we continue to provide support to him.”

A spokesperson for Jesus College, Cambridge, said it was launching its own parallel “process”. “Prof Arday’s college fellowship is linked to his university role and we will fully support the university.

“Prof Arday remains a fellow during this process. We recognise that this is a very difficult time for him and his family, and ask that they are treated with compassion and respect.”

The new investigations may have been triggered by Arday’s claims that he held a string of prestigious visiting fellowships and professorships at other universities, including statements in published biographies dating back to 2018 that he was a visiting fellow or visiting professor at Ohio State University in the US. Ohio State has denied that Arday was ever employed in any role.

Biographies linked to Arday have also claimed he had visiting professorships at Durham, Glasgow, Coventry and London Metropolitan universities as well as Nelson Mandela University in South Africa.

Arday’s appointment as professor of sociology at Cambridge, at the comparatively young age of 37, received wide publicity through Arday’s life story, which includes a diagnosis of autism at the age of three, being unable to speak until he was 11, or read or write until he was 18.

Despite those factors, Arday went on to university and swiftly climbed the academic ladder. After receiving his PhD in 2015 he held academic posts at Leeds Beckett, Roehampton and Durham universities, including a brief stint at Warwick University, before being appointed professor of sociology of education at Glasgow University in 2021. By early 2023 he had sought and won appointment to a professorship at Cambridge.

Arday also claimed to have completed 30 marathons in 35 days as well as running 600 miles in six days, and raising £5m for charity over several years. After facing questions he has revised some of those claims, and instead says he was part of a funding raising group that he cannot name for legal reasons.

Arday told the Guardian he had been the target of multiple threats after his Cambridge appointment, including having a severed pig’s head delivered to his parents’ home. Subsequent investigations found no evidence to support this claim.

The controversy comes as Simon & Schuster prepares to publish Arday’s memoir later this month, entitled Great and Unfortunate Things.

title: Texas A&M Faculty Challenge System’s Race and Gender Rules
summary:
Texas A&M Faculty Challenge System’s Race and Gender Rules
Katherine Knott Wed, 08/05/2026 - 03:00 AM
Byline(s)
Katherine Knott
full_text:
Texas A&M University faculty members sued their university this week in an effort to block a system policy that limits discussions of “race or gender ideology” on campus.

The policy, adopted last fall, required that courses “advocat[ing] race or gender ideology, sexual orientation, or gender identity” receive presidential approval. University officials have since shut down Texas A&M’s women’s and gender studies program, restricted course materials and canceled some classes.

The four faculty and the American Association of University Professors (AAUP) argue in the lawsuit, filed Monday, that the policy violates the First Amendment and their due process rights. Under the policy, faculty were barred from teaching some Plato writings and screening Moonlight, a queer coming-of-age story.

The lawsuit argues in part that the policy doesn’t make clear “what may or may not be taught, assigned, or said in a classroom, and allows virtually unfettered enforcement discretion such that disfavored viewpoints can be censored.” They want a federal judge to declare the policy unconstitutional.

Leonard Bright, a professor of public service and administration and president of the Texas A&M chapter of the AAUP, had his course canceled this past spring. He’s one of the named plaintiffs.

“This policy has impacted my ability to do my job, my students’ ability to learn, and my colleagues’ ability to teach without fear of reprisal,” he said in a statement. “The chilling effect of this policy is vast and immeasurable, and it poisons the very soul of what a university should be: a place where ideas are free to roam, and debate is uninhibited by the political winds.”

The AAUP is also suing the Texas Tech University system over similar policies and is seeking a preliminary injunction blocking two memos that outline new curricular reviews and course content guidelines. System lawyers opposed the motion for a preliminary injunction, arguing that what faculty teach in the classroom is not protected by the First Amendment.

“While TTUS faculty have First Amendment rights in connection with many of their non-classroom activities, the courses TTUS pays them to teach, and their speech in teaching those courses, is their employer’s speech and is not protected by the First Amendment,” Texas Tech’s lawyers wrote.

title: How HBCUs Help Students Find Their Way Back to College
summary:
How HBCUs Help Students Find Their Way Back to College
Joshua.Bay Wed, 08/05/2026 - 03:00 AM

InsideTrack’s five-year coaching initiative across 39 HBCUs helped stopped-out students return and stay on track toward degree completion.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
Historically Black colleges and universities have seen growing interest from students and increased investment in their missions in recent years. But for many HBCUs, longstanding resource challenges and the barriers students face outside the classroom continue to create obstacles to college completion.

A new report from InsideTrack found that a five-year coaching initiative across 39 HBCUs boosted attainment among both current and stopped-out students. Stopped-out students who received coaching re-enrolled at a rate of 6.9 percent—2.5 times the national average—with more than 1,300 returning to their institutions during the five-year period.

Among actively enrolled students, those who met with a coach retained at a rate of 90.4 percent from fall to spring, compared with 82.4 percent for students who did not complete a coaching meeting.

The report from the national student success coaching nonprofit tracked outcomes from fall 2021 through spring 2026, during which coaches supported nearly 44,000 students across the 39 campuses. They included more than 23,000 students who had stopped out before completing a degree and nearly 12,000 enrolled students navigating barriers to persistence, including balancing work and family responsibilities, financial challenges, and adjusting to college.

Coaches used personalized outreach and one-on-one sessions to help students clarify their goals, identify barriers, and navigate financial, academic and administrative challenges that could interrupt their paths to completion.

Henri LaSane, associate vice president of HBCU programs at InsideTrack, said the initiative was built around the understanding that students’ paths to completion are rarely linear and that institutions must provide support when challenges arise.

“When we look at the journey and the life cycle of a student, it’s not a straight line,” LaSane said. “Unexpected curves happen, and those things can oftentimes derail and unintentionally impact our belief and ability to re-enroll and persist.”

Rebuilding student momentum: LaSane said many HBCU students cited two common areas of struggle: finances and a sense of belonging. While HBCUs often provide students with a strong sense of community, belonging can still be complicated as students adjust to college life, he said.

“One of those underrated things that happens with belonging is being homesick,” LaSane said. “I don’t think we speak enough about how much of a role being homesick plays into a young person’s sense of belonging on any kind of campus.”

“There’s an assumption that because we are attracting Black students to a Black campus that they’re going to automatically experience this sense of belonging,” he added. “But there’s also still cultural dynamics.”

In addition, many students found financial pressures challenging, LaSane said, as they sought to balance their education with family responsibilities and other obligations outside the classroom.

“Considering that most of the backgrounds and demographics of the learners that we bring in are normally coming from under-resourced communities, family dynamics oftentimes play a role where some of these learners are contributing financially to their household,” LaSane said. “We know that the collegiate journey is a delayed gratification journey, and there are immediate needs and stressors that are being presented to us.”

The report found that the multi-year coaching initiative focused much of its outreach on students who are often overlooked by traditional retention efforts, including adult learners, who made up nearly 40 percent of the coached population, and Black male students, who made up about a third.

Among a subset of 13 public HBCUs, Black male students who met with a coach re-enrolled at a rate of 15.1 percent—10.8 percentage points higher than their peers from the same cohort who did not meet with a coach.

LaSane said many Black male students have not always seen higher education as a space where they feel supported or valued, making relationship-building a critical component of re-engagement efforts.

“Higher ed resonates a little bit differently for Black males, where I think there was a message of value that has shifted, and institutions did not shift accordingly,” LaSane said. “Coaching, I believe, lays that out for them in a way that provides some individualized attention that has been sorely missing within the Black male landscape.”

Strengthening HBCU support: The initiative was part of a broader effort to support HBCUs, which make up just 3 percent of the nation’s colleges and universities yet produce nearly 20 percent of all Black graduates, data shows.

The five-year initiative was made possible through a coalition of funders and partners, including Blue Meridian Partners, UNCF’s Institute for Capacity Building, the Thurgood Marshall College Fund and Ed Advancement. The coaching was delivered by a team of seven partnership directors and 28 trained success coaches, nearly all of whom were HBCU alumni.

Julian Capel, director of partnership development at Ed Advancement, said the outcomes challenged assumptions about students who stop out, emphasizing that many have the ability to succeed when they receive sustained support.

“I love the fact that, despite what the narratives are out there about HBCUs or Black and brown students, we’re more than capable,” Capel said. “Sometimes they need a level of support that they didn’t even know they needed.”

Of the students who received outreach from a coach, more than 2,300 have gone on to graduate, according to outcomes verified through the National Student Clearinghouse. Participating institutions also saw an estimated $26.9 million in recovered and retained tuition revenue tied to students returning and continuing their education.

Capel said the long-term goal is to help HBCUs build sustainable systems of support that remain in place beyond the initial coaching intervention.

“There’s constant turnover at HBCUs. There’s constant people shifting, but if you have the right people in place, it’s kind of like sports,” Capel said. “If you set the culture the right way, it doesn’t matter which players come in here because we’re going to win regardless.”

title: Where Enrollment Stands as Fall 2026 Approaches
summary:
Where Enrollment Stands as Fall 2026 Approaches
Johanna Alonso Wed, 08/05/2026 - 03:00 AM

Although six in 10 enrollment leaders said their colleges had met their fall 2026 enrollment goals, that number was lower for small colleges, which also discounted more and relied on campus visits to convert prospective students.

Byline(s)
Johanna Alonso
full_text:
As the fall semester fast approaches, just half of small colleges are confident in their ability to meet their enrollment goals this year, according to a survey of 134 higher education enrollment leaders Niche conducted this July.

Although 61 percent of respondents told Niche they anticipated hitting those goals this fall, that number was significantly lower—50 percent—for colleges with less than 2,000 students. Leaders at smaller institutions were also more likely than their peers to say that their confidence in their ability to hit their enrollment goals had declined since earlier in the admissions cycle.

Niche’s State of Higher Education Pulse Survey, provided exclusively to Inside Higher Ed, follows a February survey that asked enrollment leaders to predict how fall 2026 enrollment would play out. The latest update highlights where enrollment stands ahead of the start of the new academic year. The report emphasizes the unique struggles of small institutions, which made up almost half of the survey sample, to differentiate themselves from other institutions and meet their enrollment goals. In recent years, several small colleges have closed raising questions about what those who remain open need to do to stay afloat.

“It’s so clear that small institutions and everybody else really face different problems, and they serve different functions, as well … they may not have as big of an enrollment goal to meet, but they have far less wiggle room, so every seat counts,” said Allison Shrivastava, an economist at Niche.

The report explores what strategies institutions used to secure their incoming classes this year. Across the board, respondents cited campus visits as the most important strategy, followed by faster, clearer financial aid packages and parent engagement. Campus visits were especially valuable to smaller colleges, with 92 percent of respondents at institutions with fewer than 2,000 students listing them as a top lever for securing students.

The report notes that relying too heavily on any one tool can be risky: “One small school named its single biggest unsolved problem simply as the decline in campus visits, while others tied lack of event engagement directly to melt.”

Fewer institutions—just 22 percent—listed “increased discounting” as an important lever, and those who selected that option were less likely to hit their targets than their peers. Niche researchers argued that this indicates that quicker and clearer aid offers are more important than the amount of aid.

But Bob Massa, a retired enrollment manager with 45 years of experience in the field, argued that that’s not the case.

“To say that the amount of discounts, the amount of scholarships, is secondary, is simply not true,” said Massa, vice president emeritus of enrollment and college relations at Dickinson College. “The survey did not ask how big those aid increases were, nor how much aid was originally offered, making it difficult to know exactly why the offers of increased aid were less successful at helping institutions hit their enrollment goals.

Overall, smaller institutions also offered much more in discounts than larger institutions, with a median discount rate of 63 percent at institutions with fewer than 2,000 students versus 34 percent at institutions with over 5,000 students.

The results showed mixed signals about whether higher discounts led to improved enrollment outcomes. Institutions that expected to hit their targets had slightly higher median freshman discounts than those who expected to fall short. But those that expected to exceed their goals discounted slightly less than those who merely reached their target. Meanwhile, only about half of institutions that relied on “increased discounting” this year (48 percent) hit their deposit targets, versus 67 percent of those who said they did not lean on increased discounting.

Massa said he would’ve been interested in seeing how discounting impacted not only institutions’ enrollments but also their revenues.

“You can meet your enrollment goal and be very short on net revenue if you discount too much. On the other hand, you can come in low on your enrollment and, because your discount rate was lower, you can actually meet your revenue goals,” he added. “It’s not that one is more important than the other—you need the students for a vibrant community, you need the students to fill different majors. All of that is important. But if you don’t have the revenue, you really can’t fulfill the promise.”

The survey also asked institutions to describe their biggest unsolved enrollment challenge. The most common type of problem, cited by 30 percent of institutions, had to do with brand recognition and differentiation, with one respondent noting that, “our competitors are seemingly everyone." Colleges that increased their marketing budgets were also more likely to meet their enrollment goals than those who held steady or decreased those budgets.

A quarter said yield was their biggest issue. Just 18 percent of respondents said affordability; that number was slightly higher (20 percent) among small and midsized schools, but much smaller (8 percent) among institutions in the Northeast.

“For schools in the Northeast, cost barely registers; the fight is for attention,” the report stated.

Despite this, Massa noted the questions of brand recognition and affordability are one and the same, to some extent; colleges have to have a strong enough reputation for their price tag to make sense to students.

title: Vanderbilt’s Board Declares War Against Academic Freedom
summary:
Vanderbilt’s Board Declares War Against Academic Freedom
sara.custer@in… Wed, 08/05/2026 - 03:00 AM

A new policy punishes faculty for speech the trustees deem strays from the core purpose of the university.

Byline(s)
John K. Wilson
full_text:
On July 29, Vanderbilt University’s board of trustees announced the release of “The University And Its Purpose: A Declaration of First Principles.” Under the guidance of Chancellor Daniel Diermeier, this declaration marks an alarming threat to free expression and represents the worst attack yet by a Board of Trustees against academic values.

Last month, I warned that the so-called Vanderbilt Report on scholarship in the humanities and the social sciences seemed to embrace the “first steps” toward authoritarian answers to its (badly) alleged crimes against academic standards. Little could I imagine that the explicit march toward censorship would come so quickly at Vanderbilt.

The Vanderbilt board goes far beyond mere criticism of faculty with views they dislike, to claiming that professors with views they deem “political” are violating their professional duties: “Faculty have a corresponding duty to act in accordance with and actively maintain scholarly standards. Faculty fail to live up to this duty if they individually or collectively (e.g., in academic units or scholarly associations) subordinate scholarly standards to a political and social agenda.”

This standard is extraordinarily dangerous to academic freedom because it endorses punishing faculty if they are deemed to have a “political and social agenda,” whatever that means.

The Vanderbilt board expands this threat against any faculty deemed to promote evil political ideas in class discussions: “Faculty—individually and through academic units—fail in their responsibility if course offerings, syllabi, or class discussions suppress or promote ideas and perspectives that are rooted in political or personal commitments as opposed to academic merit.” There is nothing wrong with promoting perspectives that have political commitments; in fact, intellectual diversity requires this, because some viewpoints include political commitments.

Yet, the alleged evil of a political opinion is seen by the Vanderbilt board to justify extreme repression of academic norms and standards: “When academic units deviate from these commitments, academic leaders need to address such dysfunction through standard academic processes such as replacement of leadership; reorganization of units, including receivership and closure; the creation of new units; or focused hiring and educational initiatives.”

My answer to these proposals is: No, no, no, no, and no.

Absolutely none of these extraordinary measures are “standard academic processes.” They are clear attacks on shared governance and academic freedom, and they are direct violations of institutional neutrality because the administration is favoring one ideological side in academic disputes over another.

Let’s take them in order:

“Replacement of leadership”: Department chairs should be elected by the members of a department. A department chair can be removed via due process if they commit misconduct, but taking a political position is not misconduct, and the administration should not get to determine any replacements because departments should elect their leaders.

“Reorganization of units”: This term is unclear, but it seems to indicate rearranging departments in order to destroy one that allows views the administration opposes. Reorganizations of units rarely serve any useful purpose, and should only be done with faculty consultation and approval.

“Receivership and closure”: Receivership typically refers to a situation where internal conflicts within a department are so extreme that temporary outside leadership is needed to ensure the functioning of the program. Closure is an extreme action justified only by financial crisis or purely academic standards. Receivership and closure should never be a response to complaints about political agendas, and any action of this kind should require university-wide faculty approval.

“Creation of new units”: Universities can create new academic units with faculty approval based on important academic goals. However, colleges should never create duplicate departments for ideological reasons designed to replicate and then replace departments.

“Focused hiring and educational initiatives”: Hiring that is “focused” seems to mean giving preference to conservatives, perhaps by focusing on subfields perceived to have more right-leaning members. This is highly inappropriate and such politically motivated hiring should never be imposed on departments. (Voluntary educational initiatives, on the other hand, can legitimately aim at widening the diversity of viewpoints as part of legitimate academic goals.)

An institution must remain neutral with regard to the ideological beliefs of its faculty. A college does not hire based on ideology, and an administration must not manipulate the ideological composition of its departments, even when it dislikes the ideology of some professors.

The Vanderbilt board claims that it is implementing its devotion to institutional neutrality, and compels it to an extraordinary degree: “the university will implement a policy of institutional neutrality that requires university leaders at all levels to abstain from actions or speech relating to political and social matters that are not directly connected to its core purpose.”

This means that all university leaders—including program heads and department chairs—will be banned from any speech at any time discussing any political matters that the board deems to stray from the core purpose.

Institutional neutrality does not require silencing university leaders at all levels; in fact, such silencing is a violation of institutional neutrality, since it requires the institution to intervene and censor speech deemed too political by the powers that be.

Faculty in the classroom and department chairs speaking anywhere about anything are not the only ones at Vanderbilt who will have to watch what they say. Some of the worst proposals for repression by the Vanderbilt board are aimed at foreign scholars.

One alarming part of the Vanderbilt board’s declaration is its stark xenophobia. According to Vanderbilt, “Universities will endeavor to expand access and opportunity for American students, consistent with their academic standards and institutional mission.” But giving preference to American students is directly contrary to principles of academic merit.

But much worse is how Vanderbilt plans to treat foreign students or scholars: “Upon learning that a foreign entity or individual is operating with malign intent or counter to American interests, institutions have an obligation to act swiftly and transparently in severing that relationship.”

The Trump administration’s attacks on international students and scholars have caused devastating destruction to American universities. But this marks the first time a research university has deliberately harmed itself by adopting anti-foreigner rules even more repressive than the Trump regime.

These undefined terms mean that almost anything—including political opinions—could be deemed “malign” in some way or “counter to American interests.” Vanderbilt’s standards are even vaguer than the similar excuses invoked by Secretary of State Marco Rubio (“undermine the foreign policy objectives or compromise the national security interests of the United States") to ban international students for their political opinions. At least the Trump administration only claimed that “national security interests” could justify banning a foreigner; Vanderbilt expands that to any “American interests.” Vanderbilt’s declaration creates a segregated code of conduct, where a university openly announces that foreign students and staff have far fewer rights to free speech on campus than Americans do.

The attack on a “foreign entity” is also alarming because there’s a term for this: academic boycotts. In fact, no other board at an American college has ever openly espoused such a clear standard for boycotting Israel as this statement. All you have to do is argue that Israel’s government has a “malign intent” in killing thousands of people in Gaza, or that the war Israel instigated with Iran is “counter to American interests”—which a strong majority of Americans now believe—and this statement requires Vanderbilt to completely sever any relationship they have with Israel—which would mean divestment from Israel, ending Vanderbilt’s relationship with the Israel Antiquities Authority, and the deplatforming of high-level Israeli officials who often speak at Vanderbilt.

As a critic of all academic boycotts, I completely oppose the tactics of the boycott, divestment and sanction (BDS) movement (while strongly supporting people’s rights to advocate them), but even the worst proposal by BDS advocates has never gone so far as the Vanderbilt plan in its potential repression.

No university board has ever done more to undermine its status as a global entity than the Vanderbilt board in this declaration. Why would any foreign citizen work or study at Vanderbilt knowing that they can be dismissed for saying anything “counter to American interests”?

The idea that anyone would celebrate this xenophobic assault by a university on the free speech rights of foreign students and faculty and attack on everyone’s academic freedom is baffling to me. Yet Heterodox Academy praised the Vanderbilt Declaration for “its continuing efforts to steer the sector in principled leadership.”

Stanford Alumni for Free Speech and Critical Thinking declared that the Vanderbilt declaration is “an extraordinarily well written statement of everything we and others have long been urging for Stanford and other colleges and universities throughout the country. We suggest that Stanford’s senior administration and Trustees shouldn’t waste time writing their own statement but should just adopt this statement exactly as written.”

title: From Knowledge Building to Wisdom Building in Higher Education
summary:
From Knowledge Building to Wisdom Building in Higher Education
jdimaggio@upcea.edu Wed, 08/05/2026 - 03:00 AM

In years gone by, we said that students went to college to gather knowledge. Now, college is appropriately expected to be much more about building wisdom.

Byline(s)
Ray Schroeder
full_text:
The expectations of prospective students and families, employers and society at large have shifted. Knowledge and information have become instantaneously available at speeds approximating personal recall. The next step in the process is to cultivate wisdom in recommending or taking action on available knowledge. Our primary mission has shifted over the past quarter century. This is at the core of our raison d’être in higher education. The definition of what it means to “educate” those who come to us has changed. It is important for us to reflect on what these changing expectations mean in the mid-21st century.

The advent of the internet toward the end of the last century went a long way to stimulate this shift to the emphasis on wisdom. More recently, artificial intelligence has further accelerated the move. Those of us in higher education who still have our focus on knowledge gathering in our classes are a quarter of a century behind the times. Rote memorization of facts is out of date, supplanted by highly refined search and retrieval skills coupled with an ability to apply sophisticated critical and creative thinking to those data.

It may seem to be a subtle difference between knowledge and wisdom. Traditionally, we have said that knowledge is the foundation of wisdom. Meriam-Webster lists as its first definition of knowledge: “information, understanding, or skill that you get from experience or education.” Whereas the Cambridge Dictionary begins its definition of wisdom by referencing knowledge: “the ability to use your knowledge and experience to make good decisions and judgments.”

Most Popular

Knowledge can lead to wisdom, so, what’s the big deal? It is a big deal to differentiate the process of memorization and regurgitation of facts or information, and the sophisticated synthesizing of plans and action based upon metacognitive critical and creative thought to achieve wisdom.

The nature of knowledge has evolved over the years. In prior centuries, those seeking wisdom would begin by supplementing their brain-based memories with personal libraries which served as a sort of extended memory for the decision-making process. We developed encyclopedias, almanacs, indexes, readers’ guides to periodicals and related tools to provide shortcuts to useful, handy knowledge and information. The advent of the World Wide Web in 1993 with the first effective, universally accessible graphical browser, Mosaic, created our personal extended knowledge index to an incredibly massive, constantly expanding library of information.

With nimble fingers, a robust internet connection and advanced skills for efficient information retrieval from the best online sources, our cranium-contained memory is supplemented by the awesomely expansive virtual memory of the internet. In effect, the internet has become an extension of our brain. Vastly larger than the largest library, it offers retrieval technologies that perform at speeds and accuracy rivaling physical memory recall. In many instances, the internet provides more reliable and more complete results than knowledge that is naturally stored in our own aging brains.

Our next step in expectations that are placed on colleges and universities is cultivating a relationship between our learners and AI. This is somewhat more challenging, given the incredibly rapid continuing development of AI technologies. The pace is head-spinning to say the least. Performance benchmarks are set periodically, but these must constantly be revised because capabilities expand beyond those that can possibly be measured using older benchmarks. New versions of AI systems are released three or four times a year; while each version sets a new conceptual standard for capabilities.

It’s no wonder that college students and their prospective employers are clamoring for greater awareness and deeper understanding of AI among graduates. Alcino Donadel of University Business last month reported on the recently released Coursera study of the ten foundational AI skills sought by students and employers alike:

These changes in expectations demand that we find ways to integrate wisdom-building practices and AI utilizations into our curricula. These are both best accomplished if they are part of every class that we offer. It is not good enough to have a single AI Applications course; rather we should use AI in every class so that interacting with generative and agentic AI becomes a comfortable and effective activity for students. It should be an everyday experience.

Building wisdom should also become a natural experience. Applying the principles of creative and critical thinking should be equally natural. Some examples of exercises that employ these skills are enumerated by Australian Christian College:

To best serve our students, we should provide portfolio software in which they can display assignments and other projects that demonstrate such skills, especially as they relate to their desired careers. In doing so, we can focus our learning outcomes and position our students to best demonstrate their preparedness for launching their careers. We can also facilitate internships in relevant fields and offer experiential assignments that engage students with professionals in their field of study.

We are at the turning point in higher learning where we must now shift our focus from memorization and recitation of facts to the synthesis and analysis of a much broader virtual “library” of knowledge. From this perspective, we will build wisdom among our students. This new level of learning will provide the platform for graduates and certificate completers to exercise leadership and vision in our society.

title: Antisemitism on campus is 'systemic' and going unaddressed, says new report
full_text:
A national report documenting antisemitism on Canadian university and college campuses has found an "alarming prevalence" of the prejudicial behaviour across the country along with a widespread failure to address the problem.

"The findings indicate that many Jewish students experience widespread and persistent antisemitism on Canadian campuses as a defining feature of post-secondary life that shapes their behaviour, their ability to fully participate in campus life, their safety and their well-being," the report said.

The report is the first of two commissioned by the federal government's former special envoy on preserving Holocaust remembrance and combatting antisemitism. The second report will look at the general student population's views on antisemitism.

They combine the results of two surveys, one that spoke to 900 Jewish students attending post-secondary institutions across the country and another that spoke to 755 non-Jewish students "from the broader campus population."

The surveys conducted from Nov. 17 to Dec. 19 last year found that 95.7 per cent of Jewish students had experienced or witnessed at least one antisemitism incident in the previous 12 months.

The report also said 18 per cent of those events were perceived by the victim to have been caused by faculty members, while another seven per cent involved teaching assistants.

One student, who has not been named in the report, said a "professor wrote that we should kill all Zionists, that she's worked with them and sees how evil they are."

Another student reported a professor saying "Hitler was a hero" while another said a professor told them "Jews belong in Poland and need to go back."

Jewish students also reported numerous instances of faculty bias, one-sided accounts of complex issues and teaching assistants pressuring students whose work they were marking to attend pro-Palestinian demonstrations.

'Neither isolated or episodic'

Another student said a women and gender studies professor gave her zero per cent on an assignment because it addressed sexual assaults by Hamas on Jews during the Oct. 7, 2023, attack.

The student at the heart of this incident said the professor told them to instead focus on "Israeli police's role in sexual assaults."

"The central finding here is very clear: Antisemitism on Canadian campuses is neither isolated or episodic … it can reasonably be described as systemic," Jack Jedwab, the report's principal author, said in Ottawa on Wednesday.

"There's no qualifiers for this antisemitism, there's no adjectives, there's no pretext for it," said Jedwab, the president and CEO of the Association for Canadian Studies and Metropolis Institute.

A third of students who said they witnessed or experienced an antisemitic incident reported it to the university, but 63 per cent of those who filed a report said they were dissatisfied with how it was handled.

Overall 70 per cent of the Jewish students surveyed reported feeling that the university does not take the issue seriously, and 68 per cent said campus life is not safe or inclusive for Jewish students.

"Jewish students report changing what they say, where they go, what they wear and whether they remain engaged in academic and campus life at all," the report said.

The number of antisemitic incidents in Canada have spiked since the start of the Israel-Hamas war, with synagogues being shot at or firebombed and Jewish-owned businesses targeted. Members of Canada's Muslim community have also experienced Islamophobic attacks against places of worship and businesses over the same period.

The Israeli military's nearly three-year operation in Gaza has killed over 70,000 people, according to the Gaza Health Ministry and human rights organizations.

The war erupted with the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel that killed over 1,000 people and took about 250 hostage.

In response to the findings of the report, the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs, B'nai Brith Canada and the Friends of Simon Wiesenthal Center issued a joint statement calling for action.

"We call on university leaders and governments at every level to carefully consider this report," the statement said. "The drivers of this hatred — including antizionism — are well known, and the time to act is now. We need concrete actions to protect Canadian students."

This report was released on the same day as U.S.-based think-tank Jewish Tulsa garnered attention for pressuring U.S. President Donald Trump to offer refugee status to Jewish Canadians that feel threatened by rising antisemitism.

"With the urgency around the challenges and the inaction we see in Canada, an asylum pathway makes sense," Jewish Tulsa's executive director Joe Roberts told The Canadian Press.

Roberts was born in Ohio but moved to Canada in 2016 in part because he feared democratic backsliding under the Trump administration.

When antisemitic graffiti started popping up in his local park in 2023, Roberts said he decided to move to Tulsa.

Roberts said a group in Tulsa that helps Jewish people settle in the city has received inquiries from 800 to 900 Jewish Canadian families representing roughly 2,000 people who say they are considering leaving Canada.

Most of the Canadians able to make such a move either qualify for a visa under the North American trade agreement CUSMA or are eligible for American citizenship through family or marriage ties, Roberts said.

title: Australia: Pearson launches International Student Advisory Board
summary:
Pearson has launched an International Student Advisory Board, bringing together student leaders from across Australia to shape conversations on education and employability.

The post Australia: Pearson launches International Student Advisory Board appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Pearson’s International Student Advisory Board (ISAB) will serve as a platform to amplify student voices and strengthen collaboration between students, education providers, industry and government, the organisation said in a statement announcing its launch.

The ISAB will seek to introduce practical recommendations more directly into sector conversations about student success, employability and belonging.

The Board brings together a group of recognised international student leaders, advocates and community connectors with lived experience of studying, working and building a life in Australia.

“International students bring enormous talent, ambition and perspective to Australia,” said Matthew Lampkin, director, PTE Asia-Pacific.

“Through the International Student Advisory Board, we want to elevate the student voice and create a practical forum where their lived experience can help inform better decisions across education, employability and community participation.”

Speaking to The PIE News, Lampkin said that one of the reasons for the creation of the ISAB was to ensure that students remain “at the front and centre” of the organisation’s offering.

Members include current and former international student ambassadors, student council leaders, national student representatives, award winners, peer mentors, content creators and public speakers.

Collectively, they bring experience across student advocacy, university leadership, community engagement, employability, peer support and international student storytelling.

“International students should have a genuine voice in the decisions that shape their journeys,” said Ojaswi Shrestha, ISAB member and student at the University of Western Australia.

Ngou Cheng (Ocean) Vong from the University of Melbourne hopes that “through Pearson’s global reach and influence, we can elevate international student voices, encourage more meaningful conversations, and help institutions better understand how they can support international students not only to succeed academically, but also to thrive, feel a sense of belonging, and contribute meaningfully to their communities”

Pearson said this breadth of experience is central to the Board’s purpose, not only in surfacing student perspectives, but in translating those perspectives into constructive recommendations for institutions, employers, professional bodies, government and the wider sector.

Rather than treating student voice as a one-off consultation, the Board is designed as an ongoing forum for students to share what helps them succeed, where barriers remain, and how the sector can better support international students from pre-arrival through to study, work and community participation.

The first ISAB insight paper has been released, titled ‘From Proficiency to Participation’, and highlights how how confidence, Australian communication styles, cultural context, academic participation, belonging and trusted navigation can shape whether students are able to use their English confidently after arrival.

It also asks whether the sector is creating enough meaningful opportunities for students to use their English in real academic, social and professional settings, from tutorials and group work to placements, workplaces, friendships and everyday life.

Pearson said the Advisory Board will continue to meet and generate student-led insights and recommendations for the sector.

title: Lessons from Queensland’s K‑12 international leaders
summary:
From agent relationships to offshore delivery, school leaders at The PIE High shared what’s shaping international education in Queensland’s schools.

The post Lessons from Queensland’s K‑12 international leaders appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Here are five key takeaways from the K-12 leadership roundtable at this year’s PIE High Asia Pacific conference:

1. Agents are partners, not pipelines

Michelle Waters, head of international admissions & partnerships at St Aidan’s Anglican Girls’ School, was crystal clear that relationships with agents live or die on trust and transparency. She stressed the importance of proactive, human contact rather than just transactional emails.

“I’ve learnt in this role to be very honest and upfront… saying, ‘Hey, I’ve heard this is happening – can we talk about that?’”

Her team hosts agent morning teas, invites agents onto campus, and sends regular photos and documents to help them tell the school’s story. The message: if you want quality students, you need quality relationships.

2. Teacher shortages could reshape what growth looks like

For Helensvale State High School principal Rachel Cutajar teaching is “the greatest job on earth” – but right now “is not really being able to be recruited very well”.

She noted that this reality is making decisions about international enrolments “very real” for schools as they work to support both domestic and international students.

Cutajar framed this not as a reason to pull back from international education, but as a reminder that any growth has to be realistic about teacher supply and focused on maintaining a high‑quality experience for every student.

3. Wellbeing, “hidden luggage” and the reality of global school communities

Principals also pointed to mental health as a growing pressure point. They described “incredibly brave” young people travelling across the globe without family, but schools are discovering “hidden luggage” only once students are on campus and struggling.

Cultural stigma, fears about disclosure and uneven information flows between families, agents and schools all play a role. The response from leaders is to deepen pastoral care, tighten expectations with partners and make sure support structures are robust enough for the realities of today’s cohorts.

At John Paul College, principal Craig Merritt argued that schools also need to move beyond a simple “domestic vs international” lens when they talk about student needs, pointing instead to the “breadth and complexity” of a community where more than half of families have a language background other than English.

4. Transnational education opens up – and partnerships move centre stage

While public schools have had a pathway for TNE for some time, Queensland private schools only received the “rubber stamp” from mid‑June to deliver offshore, noted Michael Bos, director of international at the Moreton Bay Colleges.

“This presents a lot of opportunities for us now, which is fantastic… but obviously, we’re behind a lot of the other states, we’re behind a lot of other countries as well,” said Bos.

The opportunity is huge – but Michael warned it hinges on choosing the right overseas partners who understand both their own regulatory frameworks and Queensland’s.

On the topic of partnerships, Brisbane Boys’ College headmaster Andre Casson argued for deeper partnerships closer to home, suggesting Southeast Queensland universities should be true partners for schools, giving international families clear, high‑quality post‑school pathways in the region.

5. Global competition is real – and international students know their options

A.B. Paterson College principal Joanne Sheehy warned that international families aren’t just comparing one Australian school with another – they are weighing up very different education systems around the world.

After visiting schools in Singapore, Shanghai, Vietnam, the Emirates and the UK, she said she has seen first‑hand how quickly some overseas schools are changing their teaching and learning, and how “articulate” international students are about their expectations.

title: From local pilot to national movement: scaling hackathons for sustainability education in Wales
summary: The post From local pilot to national movement: scaling hackathons for sustainability education in Wales appeared first on Advance HE UK.
full_text:
Dr Samantha Burvill and colleagues from Swansea University share insights into the development of their Pan Wales Future Generations Hackathon with the hope of scaling its use across the UK and beyond. The hackathon uses challenge-based learning to engage students with sustainability and Welsh policy priorities. Beginning as a local pilot in 2025, it expanded nationally, developing employability skills, fostering innovation, strengthening collaboration, and generating impactful solutions to societal challenges.

In today’s rapidly changing world, it is increasingly important students understand the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and recognise their role in addressing complex societal challenges. Universities therefore have a responsibility to equip graduates with the competencies needed to contribute to a more sustainable future.

Within Wales, this agenda is shaped by distinctive political and educational contexts. The Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015 (WFGA) is the first legislation of its kind in the world, requiring public bodies to consider the long-term impact of their decisions on social, cultural, economic and environmental wellbeing. The Act establishes seven wellbeing goals and provides a framework for creating a more sustainable and prosperous Wales.

Despite its significance, awareness of the Act among students and some organisations remains limited. Capacity constraints can also make it challenging to provide widespread support for embedding its principles. This creates an opportunity for higher education to play a more active role in connecting students with Wales’s future generations agenda.

Why Hackathons?

Hackathons offer a powerful mechanism for bringing sustainability challenges to life. Traditionally associated with computing and engineering, they are increasingly recognised as valuable pedagogic tools across disciplines.

In a hackathon, students work collaboratively to develop solutions to real-world challenges within a defined timeframe. Teams are often interdisciplinary, enabling participants to combine different perspectives and experiences. Through ideation, problem-solving and presentation, students develop creativity, communication, teamwork and enterprise skills while tackling authentic challenges.

Swansea University Humanities Hackathon 2025: A Pilot with Purpose

In March 2025, Swansea University delivered its first Humanities Hackathon centred on the Well-being of Future Generations Act 2015. Students selected one of the seven wellbeing goals and developed an innovative solution to address it.

The event was designed to increase awareness of the WFGA while empowering students to contribute practical ideas that could inform policy and practice. For participants, the legislation became more than a framework; it became a catalyst for creativity, problem-solving and civic engagement.

The winning team developed Horizon Scan Cymru, a mobile-first social enterprise concept designed to empower citizens to protect Wales’s coastal biodiversity. By enabling real-time reporting of ecological change, the platform aims to connect community knowledge with scientific and policy needs. The team have continued to develop the concept beyond the hackathon itself, highlighting its potential for enterprise and social impact.

The event also revealed that hackathons provide an effective and scalable mechanism for engaging students with the WFGA while simultaneously developing graduate skills. What began as a local pilot quickly demonstrated the potential for wider sector adoption.

Scaling Educational Innovation Across Wales

Building on the success of the pilot, the initiative evolved into a Pan-Wales Well-being of Future Generations Hackathon in 2026.

Led by Swansea University and involving every Welsh university, the competition brought students together around a shared national challenge. The first stage took place on 4 March 2026, with winning teams from each institution attending the national final hosted at Swansea University on 29 April 2026.

The national final brought together representatives from Medr, Welsh Government, Advance HE, industry, careers services, professional services and enterprise teams. It demonstrated the power of cross-sector collaboration in advancing student innovation and sustainability priorities.

Importantly, the original Swansea-winning team returned as ambassadors, contributing to event design, promotion and delivery. Their transition from participants to co-creators illustrates the value of experiential learning, highlighting how students can become active partners in shaping institutional and sector-wide initiatives.

Sector-Wide Impact

The hackathon model has already delivered a range of benefits across the Welsh tertiary education sector:

Increased awareness and understanding of the Well-being of Future Generations Act among students, staff and external stakeholders.

Strengthened collaboration between Welsh universities and key external partners.

Enhanced employability, enterprise and innovation skills through authentic challenge-based learning.

Generated new business and social enterprise concepts, including Horizon Scan Cymru and HealthBridge Wales.

Supported dissemination of good practice through Advance HE, UN PRME, the SDG Teach-In and sector conferences.

Inspired new discipline-specific initiatives, including Swansea University’s Medicine and Life Sciences Hackathon.

The development of a cross-disciplinary Hackathon Toolkit to support wider curriculum adoption.

Created opportunities for future UK-wide and international collaboration.

Looking Ahead

The Pan-Wales Well-being of Future Generations Hackathon demonstrates the transformative potential of hackathons as future-focused pedagogic tools. More importantly, it showcases how a relatively small educational innovation can be scaled into a sector-wide model that aligns student learning with national policy priorities.

By combining challenge-based learning, sustainability education and cross-sector collaboration, hackathons provide students with opportunities to develop essential employability skills while contributing to real-world social impact. The Welsh experience suggests that when universities collaborate, students can become innovators, changemakers and partners in addressing complex societal challenges.

As higher education continues to navigate an increasingly uncertain and interconnected world, such initiatives offer a practical and transferable model for embedding sustainability, creativity and civic responsibility within curricula. What began as a single institutional pilot evolved into a national movement demonstrating the powerful role higher education can play in shaping a more sustainable future for Wales and beyond. The question is how could you utilise a hackathon within your discipline or context?

full_text:
An emerging need in the college search process is the desire for belonging and community. Prospective students and families place the requirements high on their priority list. They’re online, searching for information, emotional support, and advice from people who live and look like them, wondering if they'll be welcomed and feel like they belong at the school they choose. In the post-pandemic world, conversations related to college admissions and belonging skyrocketed, with more mentions in 2024 than any of the previous four years. Finding the right fit institution is front of mind for students and their families through the decision process.

A partnership with Jeff Selingo for his book Dream School: Finding the College That’s Right For You, prompted us to explore recent online college admissions conversation. The insights and themes we uncovered prompted us to return to our analyses of the college decision-making journey over the past ten years.

Jeff Selingo’s book guides students and families to look beyond elite schools by identifying seven measurable dimensions of a “good school” that most rankings don’t capture. Campus Sonar developed actionable strategies from our research to help campuses improve their student-centric approach by focusing on recruiting and enrolling students based on individual fit, ensuring future success for students and sustainable institutions.

Actionable strategy

Improve your sense of community

The theme of belonging and community has grown year over year throughout our decade-long research, but especially within the context of mental health, cultural fit, and student support services. Cultural fit has many different meanings and is a very personal experience. Student support services might include an institution's access to healthcare, mental health services, and campus safety, both physical security and personal security.

Campus Sonar’s comprehensive recommendation is to work toward improving your sense of community, specifically with the general population. Knowing the importance of belonging, campuses need to show how students build a sense of community among themselves.

Take action: Market the human experience

Build awareness around the relationships, mentorship, and connections on campus to emphasize the sense of community.

Enrollment leaders at a public university in the Southeast wanted to understand how belonging drives undergraduate demand and drives positive enrollment outcomes.

Strategic support

With enrollment growth as a top priority, the campus sought to understand the perception of belonging and evolve how their community demonstrated belonging. A social intelligence analysis of the theme within the current student audience provided insights that helped the enrollment team support campus communicators. The findings revealed messaging opportunities to recruit and enroll a diverse first-year class in two dominant areas—mental health and student involvement. The teams used strategies such as leveraging ambassadors to share stories and increase prospective student engagement, curating student-generated content for storytelling and social media, and encouraging ambassadors to engage in subreddit conversations to build awareness of mental health and student support resources on campus, strengthening their culture of belonging.

Take action: Foster campus engagement

Create space for purposeful interactions across your campus so students have safe spaces to build meaningful relationships.

A regional public university in the South needed support building team capacity and incorporating strategic insights. They wanted to better leverage social media to create organic interest and shape the story their campus tells.

Strategic support

The university’s communications team uses social intelligence to support their brand health strategy, giving them a stronger understanding of their brand equity including how their strong sense of community is one of their areas of brand power. Social intelligence insights demonstrate how their audience responds positively to big moments as well as everyday lifestyle content. The team leans into this authenticity and highlights experiences that advance campus affinity and elevate the community dynamic we consistently see in their brand story. Capturing more in-the-moment content is a way to capture the day-to-day spirit of the campus and nurture positive feelings.

With increasing enrollment, it’s noteworthy students still credit the campus for their sense of community. The team uses actionable strategies from social intelligence to maintain their campus values. To maintain their differentiators, they amplify mentions or stories that highlight the strong sense of community. This is particularly helpful as students weigh their options within the state and beyond.

Take action: Understand perception of campus community

Use social intelligence to understand perceived versus actual student support, ensuring what you believe is true about your student support is what students actually say about it.

A medium-sized, highly ranked public university known for its “small feel” and close community wanted to understand and shape their current perception.

Strategic support

In assessing their brand equity, campus leadership learned their assumptions that the perception and experience of the campus were not validated with social intelligence. Historically leaders believed the campus was seen as “too rigorous,” but social intelligence findings revealed conversations where individuals talk about rigor alongside the level of community support and available resources, differentiators that established rigor as a positive factor.

The campus was recognized for their distinction of having a “small college” atmosphere. Students mentioned support and opportunities to connect with peers, aligning with institutional values of belonging and flourishing. The university leverages these attributes as differentiators with prospective audiences seeking a public research university with opportunities for personal connection.

title: Innovative Lehre neu denken: Wie Curricula unter Druck zukunftsfähig werden
summary: The post Innovative Lehre neu denken: Wie Curricula unter Druck zukunftsfähig werden appeared first on Hochschulforum Digitalisierung.
full_text:
Im Juni haben wir im Rahmen des University:Future Festivals unter dem Motto „Under Pressure“ gemeinsam diskutiert, gelernt und Erfahrungen ausgetauscht. Im HFD-Blog blicken wir auf die Themen zurück, die das Festival in diesem Jahr besonders geprägt haben. Im Bereich der innovativen Lehre zeigte sich vor allem, dass Hochschulen ihre Curricula neu denken müssen. Künstliche Intelligenz und gesellschaftliche Transformationen verändern die Rahmenbedingungen akademischer Bildung von Grund auf.

Die Diskussionen kreisten zunehmend um eine zentrale Frage: Welche Kompetenzen brauchen Studierende in einer Zukunft, die sich immer schneller verändert, und welche Rolle kommt Hochschulen dabei zu? Deutlich wurde, dass die Integration von KI in die Lehre dabei nur ein Teil der Antwort ist. Entscheidend ist vor allem, Curricula so weiterzuentwickeln, dass sie Studierende auf eine Welt vorbereiten, in der Anpassungsfähigkeit, Urteilsvermögen und kritisches Denken zunehmend an Bedeutung gewinnen.

Im Mittelpunkt des Panels standen Kompetenzen wie Urteilsfähigkeit, kritisches Denken, interdisziplinäre Zusammenarbeit und der konstruktive Umgang mit Unsicherheit. Fachkompetenz bleibt unverzichtbar, jedoch reicht sie allein nicht mehr aus. KI-Kompetenz wurde deshalb nicht als eigenständiges Zusatzthema verstanden, sondern als Querschnittsaufgabe, die sich durch Studium und Lehre ziehen sollte.

Dabei wurde auch deutlich, dass Hochschulen Studierende nicht auf eine Arbeitswelt vorbereiten können, in der jede Antwort bereits von einer KI geliefert wird. Ihre Aufgabe besteht vielmehr darin, Menschen zu befähigen, Probleme eigenständig zu analysieren, Technologien kritisch einzuordnen und verantwortungsvolle Entscheidungen zu treffen.

Mit dem Heilbronner Modell und dem bayerischen Tandem-Modell wurden zwei unterschiedliche Wege vorgestellt, KI-Kompetenz in Studium und Lehre zu verankern. Während der eine Ansatz auf ein wissenschaftlich begleitetes Blended-Learning-Konzept setzt, steht beim anderen die Zusammenarbeit von Lehrenden und Studierenden im Mittelpunkt.

Trotz ihrer unterschiedlichen Herangehensweisen verband beide Projekte dieselbe Überzeugung: Nachhaltige Curriculumentwicklung entsteht durch langfristige Strukturen und kontinuierliche Weiterentwicklung. Dazu gehört auch, KI-Kompetenz interdisziplinär in Curricula zu verankern und sie als Querschnittsaufgabe über Fachgrenzen hinweg zu vermitteln, statt sie auf einzelne Lehrveranstaltungen oder Studiengänge zu beschränken

Interessant war dabei auch, dass immer wieder die Zusammenarbeit zwischen Hochschulen thematisiert wurde. Viele der vorgestellten Konzepte leben davon, Erfahrungen zu teilen, Materialien gemeinsam weiterzuentwickeln und voneinander zu lernen. Curriculumentwicklung wurde damit nicht als Aufgabe einzelner Hochschulen verstanden, sondern zunehmend als gemeinsamer Lernprozess.

Katharina Scheiter machte deutlich, dass KI weder automatisch zu besseren noch zu schlechteren Lernergebnissen führt. Entscheidend sei vielmehr, wann und wie sie eingesetzt wird. Wer sich zunächst selbst mit einem Problem auseinandersetzt und KI anschließend zur Reflexion oder Vertiefung nutzt, kann davon profitieren. Erfolgt der Einsatz jedoch zu früh, besteht die Gefahr, dass wichtige Denk- und Problemlösungsprozesse gar nicht erst entstehen.

Die Diskussion verdeutlichte damit, dass innovative Curricula nicht nur neue Inhalte brauchen, sondern auch Lernumgebungen, die eigenständiges Denken weiterhin fördern. Wenn richtig eingesetzt, kann KI kann diesen Prozess unterstützen. Ersetzen kann sie ihn jedoch nicht.

Die Beiträge des University:Future Festivals machten deutlich, dass innovative Lehre heute weit mehr umfasst als digitale Werkzeuge oder neue Prüfungsformate. Hochschulen stehen vor der Aufgabe, Curricula kontinuierlich an neue gesellschaftliche, technologische und berufliche Anforderungen anzupassen.

Dafür braucht es nicht nur neue Inhalte, sondern auch geeignete Strukturen: fachübergreifende Zusammenarbeit, Raum für didaktische Experimente und eine Kultur des gemeinsamen Lernens. Viele der vorgestellten Projekte zeigten, dass nachhaltige Innovation vor allem dort entsteht, wo Hochschulen Erfahrungen teilen, Konzepte weiterentwickeln und Veränderungen strategisch begleiten.

„Under Pressure“ bedeutet in diesem Zusammenhang vor allem, Curriculumentwicklung als kontinuierlichen Prozess statt als einmalige Reformaufgabe zu verstehen. Zukunftsfähige Lehre entsteht dort, wo Hochschulen bereit sind, ihre Bildungsziele immer wieder zu hinterfragen und Veränderung als festen Bestandteil akademischer Bildung begreifen.

Marina Konno ist studentische Mitarbeiterin im Kommunikationsteam des Hochschulforum Digitalisierung. Sie studiert Kultur- und Medienwissenschaft an der Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin mit besonderem Fokus auf postkolonialen Studien, digitalen Öffentlichkeiten und gesellschaftlichen Transformationsprozessen.

Vor ihrer Tätigkeit im HFD arbeitete sie in unterschiedlichen Bereichen der Bildungs-, Kommunikations- und Digitalpraxis – unter anderem im Bundestag, bei der internationalen Jugendorganisation IJGD sowie bei Amazon. Im HFD unterstützt sie die redaktionelle und kommunikative Arbeit rund um Themen der Hochschulbildung, Digitalisierung und gesellschaftlichen Transformation.

full_text:
Qualche settimana fa, il parlamento ha approvato una riforma del reclutamento universitario che abolisce, ma solo un po’, il meccanismo dell’Abilitazione Scientifica Nazionale. Le opposizioni hanno risposto con una proposta di “concorso nazionale”. Sia la maggioranza, che l’opposizione sembrano individuare alcuni problemi del sistema, ma non si sono prese le necessarie responsabilità dello stato di cose presente, e le loro proposte non cambiano i fondamentali dell’Università e della Ricerca in Italia.

A parte le solite, necessarie, ripetute, e mai ascoltate richieste di finanziamenti (“no strings attached”) per il sistema dell’Università e della Ricerca, qui si propone la netta separazione tra reclutamento e progressioni di carriera come (una) riforma del sistema; una riforma già implementabile, anche se, ovviamente, non a costo zero, che rappresenta una soluzione parziale ai problemi più evidenti dell’Accademia. La prima questione riguarda la macchinosità e la burocratizzazione dei meccanismi di valutazione e di selezione dei singoli. Abilitazione Scientifica Nazionale (ASN) in primis. Ovvero, il finanziamento complessivo al sistema dell’Università e della Ricerca è tuttora infimo.

Sgomberato il campo dalle questioni venali, vediamo un po’ cosa succede oggi nelle Università (e, pare, negli ERP) riguardo le carriere, e dove le proposte sul tappeto convergono di fatto: la compressione dell’autonomia universitaria e della libertà accademica centrata sui Dipartimenti (full disclosure: ne dirigo uno, di Informatica).

E no, il numero di pubblicazioni (pardon: dei “prodotti per la ricerca”) non è una misura valida: chi lo sostiene dovrebbe spiegare come mai l’Italia sia più produttiva, tout court, della Cina, secondo uno studio pubblicato su PLoS One[1].

Oltre alle considerazioni fatte precedentemente, si nota però che né le forze di governo, né quelle ora di opposizione riconoscano le rispettive, e simili, responsabilità per la situazione attuale. Le forze di governo non riconoscono che la Legge Gelmini è fonte primaria dei problemi attuali, sebbene votata da loro (inclusi i predecessori di Fratelli d’Italia), mentre l’opposizione, il PD in primis, non riconosce ancora, neppure nei documenti interni, che ANVUR e l’ASN furono proposte e votate dai suoi esponenti.

La legge “Bernini” e la proposta delle opposizioni

La maggioranza ha fatto propria una proposta essenzialmente “ministeriale” dove i concorsi rimarrebbero locali ma con regole stabilite altrove e probabilmente per legge su chi e come può accedervi. Il problema è che sulle suddette regole ancora non si sa molto e, in ogni caso, una struttura come ANVUR potrebbe avere – si presume troppa – voce in capitolo. L’effetto sarebbe di non risolvere il problema principale accentrando comunque potere in questa o quella struttura e comunque comprimendo, anche mediante il sorteggio delle commissioni, l’autonomia dei dipartimenti.

L’opposizione si è dichiarata per il ritorno alla situazione pre-1998 con il “concorso nazionale” a scadenza annuale o addirittura biennale. I dipartimenti dichiarerebbero le loro necessità prima della scadenza e la commissione nazionale stilerebbe una graduatoria nazionale da cui, presumibilmente, i dipartimenti sceglierebbero. Le forze di opposizione glissano sull’enorme potere che si consegnerebbe ai ministeri per la gestione di queste elefantiache e vogoniane procedure e l’esperienza ci dice che “bloccare i concorsi” sarebbe una facile manovra governativa per fare cassa. È già successo, e la soluzione furono i giustamente vituperati, per gli addetti ai lavori, “ope legis”.

Le due proposte attaccano quindi i problemi principali della situazione attuale e favoriscono l’autonomia universitaria e la libertà accademica? In generale no.

Al mondo esiste una varietà di sistemi di reclutamento accademico, più o meno distribuiti sugli assi “centralismo” e “distribuzione”. La proposta del governo sembra promuovere la “distribuzione”, ma introduce forme di “centralismo” o di “controllo centralizzato”, specialmente attraverso ANVUR. La proposta delle opposizioni è decisamente “centralista”, con la giustificazione che “bisogna mantenere una caratterizzazione nazionale dell’Accademia”.

Ora, è mia opinione che la proposta delle opposizioni sia puramente “reattiva” e mal pensata, anche se piena di buone intenzioni. Ma qui stiamo parlando di strade; lastricate. Il “concorso nazionale” pre-1998 era un retaggio napoleonico (o cinese) e, se implementato, si presenterebbe oggi come un “unicum” (assieme alla Turchia) nel panorama OCSE. Con un ulteriore problema: la “provincializzazione” del sistema, nonostante i proclami provenienti da ANVUR e dai ministeri sull’ “internazionalizzazione”.

Una proposta operativa

Il problema principale che tutti additano è il cosiddetto “localismo” dei concorsi attuali e di quelli “distribuiti” in vigore tra il 1998 ed il 2011. Ogni discussione sui concorsi parte da lì e lì si arena. Eppure, il decreto 30 e legge 79 del 2022, nelle parti riguardanti il reclutamento universitario, già mette a disposizione dei dipartimenti un mezzo per limitare questo problema: le posizioni, in particolare quelle di Ricercatore Tenure Track (RTT), possono essere riservate a persone che abbiano avuto contratti di almeno 36 mesi (cumulativi) al di fuori dell’Ateneo, dottorato incluso.

In ogni caso, anche tenendo ferme le progressioni da ricercatore “tenure-track”, a professore associato, fino a professore ordinario (ovvero, tralasciando, al momento, le discussioni sul “ruolo unico”) i punti di intervento fondamentali sono due: la limitazione del fenomeno dell’“inbreeding” e la netta separazione tra reclutamento e progressioni di carriera.

Il fenomeno dell’“inbreeding” (ovvero dei reclutamenti degli “interni”, che, ricordiamo, sono una delle cause principali dei malumori nei dipartimenti e delle tirate giornalistiche a latere) è già risolvibile imponendo la “regola dei 36 mesi” per le posizioni RTT. Nota bene: nei paesi anglosassoni ed in Germania il problema praticamente non esiste; nel primo caso per consuetudine culturale, nel secondo per ferree (troppo) norme legislative.

Al tempo stesso, il sottoporre le promozioni a “concorso”, crea iniqui rallentamenti di carriera e dissapori tra colleghi. La soluzione in questo caso è di avere concorsi per posizioni da associato o ordinario esclusivamente per candidati esterni. Il passaggio ad associato (“tenure”) dovrebbe essere condizionato a requisiti che un dipartimento elenca al momento della entrata in servizio nel ruolo di RTT. Lo stesso dicasi per il passaggio dal ruolo di associato a quello di ordinario: al momento dell’entrata in servizio come associato un dipartimento elencherà i requisiti per il passaggio al ruolo di ordinario. La differenza è che la non concessione della “tenure” causa il decadimento dal ruolo.

Si noti che i requisiti non dovranno includere vincoli finanziari complessivi; in particolare, l’oscena clausola che accompagna dal 2010 ogni norma riguardante l’università e la ricerca (“senza aggravi per il bilancio”) va semplicemente espunta dal lessico. I requisiti per l’acquisizione della tenure e per la promozione a ordinario dovranno essere decisi dai dipartimenti, in autonomia, al massimo, ma non obbligatoriamente, tramite coordinamento a livello delle società scientifiche e del CUN. Lo stesso dicasi per le procedure di selezione, da cui eleminare inutili, e costosi, aggravi amministrativi.

Il fatto che i concorsi RTT e tutti quelli di reclutamento saranno riservati ad esterni garantirà una migliore autoregolamentazione complessiva del sistema. Dopotutto, buona parte dei sistemi esteri di riferimento adottano queste forme di organizzazione.

Una critica seria riguarda la vita delle persone. Vista l’età media attuale per l’entrata in “tenure track” (RTT) è chiaro che l’imposizione di spostarsi fisicamente può creare dei problemi ad alcuni. Si consideri però che questo passaggio avviene comunque ad un’età in cui le persone e le famiglie possono ancora essere flessibili e ci si aspetta che siano messe in atto politiche per abbassare l’età per l’entrata in “tenure track” (RTT), ad esempio, aumentando … i finanziamenti. Si noti che la proposta delle opposizioni assume che un periodo post-doc diventi “obbligatorio”, aumentando in questo modo il periodo di precariato.

Esiste però un’ulteriore ragione per procedere con gradualità. Molti giovani ricercatori hanno costruito il proprio percorso professionale sulla base delle regole attualmente vigenti. Cambiarle improvvisamente mentre stanno cercando di accedere alla tenure track sarebbe ingiusto e rischierebbe di compromettere aspettative maturate in buona fede. Per questo motivo, un eventuale requisito di mobilità all’ingresso nella tenure track dovrebbe entrare in vigore solo dopo un congruo periodo transitorio — ad esempio tre anni dall’approvazione della riforma — così da consentire a chi è già nel sistema di programmare il proprio percorso senza vedersi cambiare le regole durante la corsa.

Una seconda critica molto seria si riassume con “il sistema anglosassone ha serissimi problemi di distribuzione di risorse e di sperequazione”. UC Berkeley in California non è il “community college” di Libby, Montana e viceversa. Ma ciò dimentica che comunque già ora abbiamo enormi problemi di finanziamento e che questi si risolvono garantendo una base ragionevole (e molto generosa) per tutti: l’uguaglianza ha dei vantaggi. E la discussione sui “finanziamenti del sistema” e dei “finanziamenti competitivi per la ricerca” è un capitolo a sé stante, anche alla luce delle tendenze dei governi conservatori ad usare queste leve per sminuire l’autonomia delle istituzioni accademiche e la libertà di ricerca.

Ritengo le altre critiche meno convincenti e si raggruppano sotto due etichette. La prima ha come etichetta il “eh ma qui siamo in Italia”. La seconda è “eh ma loro sono in P” (con P che assume il valore “Slovenia”, “Corea del Sud”, “Svizzera”, “USA”, “Germania”, “Botswana”, etc., etc.). Questo tipo di argomentazioni arriva sempre nelle discussioni in cui si propone ciò che è appena stato descritto. Chi scrive, ovviamente anche per storia personale, trova queste argomentazioni … provinciali e, in fondo, piuttosto superbe nella loro pretesa di riuscire a creare in Italia un sistema “più migliore”. Specie quando poi regolarmente accompagnate da esortazioni all’“internazionalizzazione” del sistema.

Conclusioni

Concludo con una nota di cautela. Il sistema proposto è una panacea? No. Ma risolve alcuni dei problemi che a questo punto tutti ritengono pervasivi. Il sistema proposto è troppo “anglosassone”? Probabile. Ma si noti come, tra tutti i sistemi provati in Italia, quello “anglosassone” non c’è mai stato: neanche quello della stagione 1998-2010 era tale, grazie alla grande tradizione manzoniana dei nostri legislatori: l’azzeccagarbuglio; aggravato dal vogonismo. In particolare, non eliminava l’inbreeding, ma tendeva piuttosto a distribuirlo attraverso accordi tra dipartimenti.

Proviamo allora qualcosa di diverso. Facciamolo evitando sia le rigidità di alcuni modelli europei, sia le disuguaglianze che caratterizzano molti dei sistemi “anglosassoni”. L’obiettivo non è imitare un paese o un altro, ma costruire un sistema più aperto, più internazionale, meno burocratico e capace di imparare dalla propria esperienza.

In altre parole, un’università e una ricerca che respirino, siano migliori, più partecipate e collaborative.
